text: Mr. Sternwaldski once wondered which word is most responsible for the meaning of this sentence. He went dizzy, stepped into a puddle and soaked his boots.

Mr. Sternwaldski sat under a tree and listened to birds. There was a rhythm and a melody in their chirping. Then he noticed the sound of leaves in the wind, beneath that the wind around his ears, and lower still the heartbeat within them. A symphony.

…it was all about putting some order and Mr. Sternwaldski kept half waking up worrying that he would not remember and then it occurred to him that dreams were exactly like thoughts and that exact thought was like switching the light in an old basement and all the dreams ran away and hid from Mr. Sternwaldski like rats and it occurred to him that dreams and thoughts were like rats, proliferating so fast, always somewhere there, even when they pretend not to be…
Mr. Sternwaldski once drove along a motorway, lost in thoughts. He missed the right exit, lost his bearings — and all of a sudden there he was.

Mr. Sternwaldski once stood at a factory siding in Northern Bohemia: no barriers, no regular trains, just a track leading into an industrial compound that looked neither alive nor abandoned, impossible to read. Two men in orange vests stopped the traffic with red flags, and after a while a slow rail trolley appeared, pulling freight wagons with containers marked Maersk and a few Chinese and Vietnamese companies that felt oddly personal. The journey from Shanghai to this afterimage of civilization was beyond him. The trolley disappeared. The cars moved on as if nothing had happened.
Mr. Sternwaldski didn't know how to express himself. For some while, he struggled with himself. Then eased off and found out that there was no need to express himself.

Mr. Sternwaldski sat on a sand rock high above an industrial town, and a chain of thoughts slowly formed in his head. From stones and water: plants. From plants: autonomous beings. From autonomous beings back to plants — and to labs and highways — all to make the future stay put.

Mr. Sternwaldski lies in the grass and enjoys the pull of gravity pressing him into the ground. He watches the sun travel from east to west above him, then remembers the faint north–south line only his compass and the geese can read. Directions. Then an idea creeps in. What about inside? From heart to liver, head to feet, from what he can see to what he cannot. There are six of them, crossing in one body.

Mr. Sternwaldski stepped into mud and an idea formed. Mud is like data — a vast soil of what exists, and of what never will. From this soil, facts do not rise on their own. Someone must separate a cluster, give it a frame, impose an order. Only then does a fact take shape, like a plant outlined by the force that forms it. From facts we shape information, and from many such acts an informational field grows — a forest of shared patterns. But to step, to choose, to frame, to pass things on requires effort. Data, facts, and information do not supply it. The source lies elsewhere. So where does this energy come from?

Mr. Sternwaldski felt as if he were in a room slowly filling with water. It entered without noise, without urgency, as if it had always belonged there. The ceiling was low. There are times when the level of the self-evident keeps rising — words repeating words, gestures repeating gestures — until it reaches the limit of one’s ability to ask a question, the only source of fresh air. And there was little of it left.

Mr. Sternwaldski stood by the river while, somewhere behind, a bull was tearing up a meadow. In the current, you must be slightly faster than the water. On solid ground, it is better to wait and redirect the charging force. He realized there was no point in choosing between swimmer and toreador. He had to be a switch. The only mistake is to be in the wrong mode for the place you are in.

At noon, in a pub, Mr. Sternwaldski watched the Olympics. The room vibrated with effort and excitement, but he felt nothing. The emptiness pleased him. It proved he could occupy a position without emotion in a world built on them. He tried to memorize the sensation in his body — the quiet, the absence — so he could summon it when needed. The winner crossed the line with arms raised, her face driven out of shape.

Mr. Sternwaldski watched an ant trail on the pavement. For a while, he only observed — the direction, the gaps, the sudden corrections. The pattern began to make sense. He thought he could tell where the next ant would appear. Then he placed his shoe a little closer, just to see better. The line broke. What he had understood vanished the moment he stepped in.
Mr. Sternwaldski entered a room and forgot why. He suspected the room might know. It remained silent. He left, leaving the question there for the next person to step in.

A snowflake landed on Mr. Sternwaldski’s sleeve and held for a moment. A log of temperatures, turns, and collisions. Before he could read it, it dissolved. He raised his eyes and saw a glittering log file all around.

Mr. Sternwaldski watched a Japanese player warming up before a tennis match. For a second, the camera tilted upward and showed a slice of sky framed by the roof above the court. Something shifted. The rectangle of blue was the same as the one he used to see from his grandmother’s yard. The smell of dust and old wood arrived without asking.
Mr. Sternwaldski searched for Olivia Fox Caban. Did you mean Oliver Fox Cable? Ok, Oliver Fox Cable. Oliver Fox Cable does not exist, but you can create it.
Mr. Sternwaldski lifted his head above the water. The scene rearranged itself instantly. It has always been a struggle for perspective, he thought. And sometimes for a snorkel.

Each spring: put your head into a tree in full bloom. At first nothing happens, only white and silence. Then something buzzes, something flickers. Then again and again and again. Soon the whole crown hums with your head inside, white rolling and swelling, pouring back and forth. Stay. Pull your head out. Marvel.

Behind the noise of the world there is silence. Catch it. It is tuned like an old radio: first the thin whistle beneath the static, and beneath that the absolute quiet. Listen past the rustle and the roar.
First he learned to speak and pretend he knew, even when he did not. Then he learned to keep silent when he did not know. Finally he learned to keep silent when he knew and no one asked.

The rumble of a train over his head. Brakes screeched. A bus exhaled. Someone laughed too loudly. A bottle rolled on the pavement. An ambulance passed. A phone rang and rang and was not answered. Mr. Sternwaldski began a descent through the layers of noise. Below was a hum. Then a thin trembling. Under that, silence. A place to return to.
Mr. Sternwaldski stumbled over a stray opinion. “What the hell!” he swore. And a revelation came. Indeed, opinions are hell.
Land belongs to no one, thought Mr. Sternwaldski while watching the news. Everyone belongs to the land.

Once again Mr. Sternwaldski reminded himself that he had to carry on, when he suddenly realized that he had quite forgotten what exactly it was he had to carry on. At that moment gravity, as if it smiled, let loose a little.
Mr. Sternwaldski was watching white water and thought: forms flow from inner unrest and outer constraints.

Someone told Mr. Sternwaldski that bees use hexagons in their hives because it is the most effective way of filling the space. Everybody is obsessed with filling, thought Mr Sternwaldski. But if you want to be you need a great deal of emptiness around you. Every being does – even atoms. Non-being, on the other hand, can tolerate any density.
Science is just a way of talking about carefully preselected ways of coming together and going apart. Its power consists mainly in turning invisible affects into visible effects.
What does fear do? It blocks in advance the space where something might be born, so that nothing can even move there. It replaces creating with repeating.

If all the difficult people I meet are there just to teach me a lesson, it once occurred to Mr. Sternwaldski, then the world suffers only because I am such a poor student. And then a wave of compassion overwhelmed him, and his anger melted away.
